endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: To be considered fair, AI solutions require (1) parity, meaning that common measures of algorithmic performance are equal across protected subgroups; (2) calibration, meaning that outcomes are independent of protected characteristics (or class) – such as race, gender, or their proxies; and (3) anti-classification, meaning that protected characteristics are not explicitly used to make decisions.

endorsements.title: Health Equity Across the AI Lifecycle (HEAAL) framework
endorsements.issuer: Health AI Partnership; PLOS Digital Health (PMID 38723025, doi:10.1371/journal.pdig.0000390)
endorsements.quote: Additionally, it requires documenting the rationale behind the selection of these specific fairness metrics.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Use this feedback to guide the design of provenance data-tracking techniques.

endorsements.title: FUTURE-AI: international consensus guideline for trustworthy and deployable artificial intelligence in healthcare
endorsements.quote: Include application specific information relevant for fairness analysis

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Categorization should also account for how risk may stack, multiply, or attenuate based on operational context (e.g., staffing levels, shift coverage) and aggregate use (e.g., multiple AI solutions influencing the same workflow or patient population).

endorsements.title: A clinician's quick‑start guide to implementing digital health innovations in the NHS - with lessons from a UK-deployed AI stroke imaging decision-support software
endorsements.quote: Pre-specified contextualised groups of interest relevant to the use case (not limited to one protected characteristic; allow intersectionality and local context).

endorsements.title: Challenges in medical algorithmic fairness
endorsements.quote: Developers should explicitly specify choices of metrics and selection strategies and disclose how these decisions might impact disparities.

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether pre-specifying equity objectives, fairness metrics, and priority subgroups improves the detection of disparities, and no supplied study documents the hazard directly. Support for R302 rests on seven endorsements from frameworks, guidance, and commentary, two of which rate it as a must.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The seven endorsements reflect expert agreement, and agreement among frameworks is a different thing from empirical findings on whether pre-specification changes which disparities evaluators find.

Two frameworks, the CHAI Responsible AI Guide and HEAAL, state the practice as a must, and five sources rate it as a should. All seven are voluntary frameworks, guidance, or commentary. None of the supplied sources is a statute or regulation that requires documented fairness metric selection.

The NHS stroke imaging commentary calls for groups of interest that extend beyond one protected characteristic and allow for intersectionality and local context. No supplied study examines whether governance teams that pre-specify subgroups include Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients, or whether data for those groups are available to evaluate.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare fairness evaluations with and without pre-specified objectives, metrics, and subgroups, and that measure whether pre-specification changes which disparities are detected and acted on. Studies should also report how often governance teams find that evaluable subgroup data are missing and what they do in response.
commentary.underserved_note: No supplied study tests the practice in any population, so no evidence includes Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Health systems cannot yet tell from evidence whether pre-specified subgroup lists capture these groups or whether the data needed to evaluate them exist.
